newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel eyes further Telekom sale.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel eyes further Telekom sale.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Wednesday mooted plans for an early sale of Bonn's stake in Deutsche Telekom AG in an apparent bid to cut government borrowing needs in the run-up to Europe's single currency.

The news initially put the brakes on the strong rise in Telekom stock, which has soared some 40 percent since its listing in November. Shares tumbled nearly five percent in early trade before bargain hunters began buying again.

While not saying conclusively what the government planned to do with its remaining 74 percent stake in the company, Waigel gave every impression that he considered an early sale of the shares to be on the agenda.
"It is conceivable that parts of the privatisation of Telekom could be brought forward," he told reporters at a book presentation in Bonn.
"It must take place in reasonable tranches, but it is possible. I am convinced it is also in the interests of Telekom to be unshackled from the chains of state as soon as possible."
At the end of 1996 the government owned just over two billion shares in Telekom, Europe's largest telecommunications group. The IPO put 713 million new shares in public hands.
The $13 billion sale of an inital 25 percent in November had no impact on government finances as the revenues went to the company itself.

The positive development of Telekom's share price and the company's robust state of health has prompted the government to consider selling its shares in order to push down budget deficits that endanger its bid for Europe's single currency.

In its listing prospectus Telekom sought to calm any uncertainties about how the government would deal with its shares, saying "the sale by the Federal Republic of shares prior to January 1, 2000 is in principle prohibited."
It added, however, that this "could be subject to differing interpretations or changed by legislative action".

With so much uncertainty still in the air and news that the government was in fact considering an early sale of shares Telekom share prices plunged in Tokyo trade on Wednesday which carried over into early European trade.
Both Deutsche Telekom and the German government stepped in to assure the market that there would be no dumping of Telekom stock that could upset markets.

Telekom chairman Ron Sommer told the Bild newspaper in a report to appear on Thursday that he would only give his approval for disposal of the government shares in such a way that did not negatively impact the market.
"We will ensure that the interests of the nearly two million shareholders are not affected. There is complete agreement on this point between the finance minister and myself," Sommer said.

The Post and Telecommunications Ministry said in a statement: "According to the legal situation, it would only be possible to sell shares off-market with the mutual agreement of the management board of the company."
The reassurances had their desired affect.
Telekom shares rebounded in late trade and ended the day at 39.20 marks, down just 93 pfennigs and traders said the earlier fall was too severe.
"People have had some second thoughts and now believe the market has overreacted," said Josh Waiblinger, an assistant vice president of equity sales at BHF Bank in Frankfurt.
But it still leaves open the question of how Bonn could dispose of its shares.
Analysts said the government could place shares privately with institutional investors at a discount to current trading prices without introducing undue volatility into the market.

This could also satisfy some of the pent up demand from institutional investors, who were only able to buy just under half of the IPO allotment in November and are reluctant to buy shares on the market, fearing this could drive up the price. ($ = 1.705 German Marks)
